hook.text: Two students face the same math test. One thinks "I can do this." The other thinks "I'll fail." Who scores better?

buildup.text: Bandura's self-efficacy is the belief that you can succeed at a specific task. It's not general confidence.

discovery.text: High self-efficacy leads people to set harder goals, persist longer, and recover faster from setbacks.

twist.text: Self-efficacy isn't delusion. It's built from mastery experiences—actual past success is the best fuel.

climax.text: Watching someone similar succeed (modeling) and receiving specific encouragement also build it.

punchline.text: Believing you can is half of doing.

quiz.question: What is the strongest source of self-efficacy?

details.summary: Bandura's self-efficacy is the belief in your ability to succeed at a specific task. It predicts effort, persistence, and achievement better than general self-esteem. Self-efficacy builds through mastery experiences, social modeling, verbal persuasion, and managing physiological states.
details.whyItMatters: Self-efficacy is one of the strongest predictors of performance across domains. Believing you can succeed makes you more likely to try, persist, and actually succeed.
takeaways: Self-efficacy is task-specific belief in your capability
Past success is the strongest source of self-efficacy
It predicts effort, persistence, and achievement outcomes

faq.question: How does self-efficacy differ from self-esteem?
faq.answer: Self-esteem is a general feeling of self-worth. Self-efficacy is the specific belief that you can perform a particular task successfully. You can have high self-esteem but low math self-efficacy. Self-efficacy predicts behavior in specific domains far better than global self-esteem does.

faq.question: What builds self-efficacy most effectively?
faq.answer: Mastery experiences, successfully completing progressively challenging tasks, are the most powerful source. Seeing similar others succeed builds vicarious efficacy. Encouragement helps but is weaker. Managing anxiety and interpreting arousal as excitement rather than fear also boosts efficacy.
